Actual Article Body:

Unafraid of hard work, Betty Ge combined nursing shifts with studying at the ANU Medical School and raising a young family.

Login or signup to continue reading

But when Nurse Ge became Doctor Ge, she was genuinely shocked by the excessive amounts of unpaid and unrostered overtime that junior medical practitioners undertook in Canberra's hospitals.

It was about more than the money. Doctors working 16 hours or longer and then starting early the next day were a potential danger to themselves and to their patients.

"We have seen doctors who had car accidents and died after long shifts," Dr Ge said.

"And now we're seeing that we make mistakes when we're fatigued and then patient care can be endangered."

Chinese-born Dr Ge, who was chair of the Australian Medical Association's Council of Doctors of Training, became one of the leaders of a campaign which resulted in a class action lawsuit being launched in 2022.

As a migrant with a young family, why did she risk speaking out?

"I guess it's stupidity or courage, however you want to call it," Dr Ge said.

"I said, 'Look, what's the worst that could happen?'"

Dr Ge was comforted by the fact she had a secure place in a general practice training program and her career was unlikely to be harmed by her advocacy. But some colleagues training for other medical specialties were scared of facing retaliation if they were identified as campaign leaders.

In 2024, Canberra Health Services and Calvary Health Care ACT settled the lawsuit for $31 million.

Two years on, Dr Ge is the Australian Medical Association ACT President, a GP and winner of the medical category in the 2026 Asian-Australian Leadership Awards.

But she is conscious of how difficult it can be for Asian-Australian professionals to break through what has been described as the "bamboo ceiling".

A survey of past winners and finalists of the Asian-Australian Leadership Awards found 84 per cent believed they had to work harder than their non-Asian colleagues to receive the same recognition or career opportunities. And 82 per cent have felt pressure to change or downplay their cultural identity to fit in or get ahead.
